rationale: A wins because it mostly stays inside the record while still giving three real desks a reason to care. Its strongest angle, "Monzo returns to the US without the banking licence it once chased," is a clean sequel to the facts: failed license, partner bank, live launch. B has sharper teeth in places, but "Nine million UK customers, zero in the US" and "then immediately spent it on the market that beat it once" turn useful angles into overconfident copy.
gaps_in_A: "Monzo's first profitable year is paying for a second shot at America" overstates causality. The update says Monzo posted a profit and launched in the US; it does not say profit is funding the launch.

"Story type: exec-spotlight" is the wrong label for the invite-only angle. No executive is named in the update, so the story is access, rollout mechanics, or consumer product availability, not an exec spotlight.
"Reporters who covered the first failure" assumes a prior coverage trail not supplied in the update. Plausible, but still not grounded in the brief.
gaps_in_B: "then immediately spent it" is unsupported. No results date, funding source, or US spend figure is supplied.
"market that beat it once" is cute copy doing factual work it has not earned. Failure to secure a banking license is not the same as the US market beating the company.
"Nine million UK customers, zero in the US" invents a number. Invite-only launch suggests limited access, not zero customers.
"European challenger banks stalling in the US" needs outside evidence. B admits that in the proof section, but the angle still smuggles the trend into the pitch frame.
